He spoke of prohibition as a failure in Marlboro, claiming that as many as 208 liquor packages had arrived at Bennettsville in one day. He claimed it to be a failure in York also. It suited the rich man, who could order his liquor all right; but the poor man, who had to depend upon the blind tiger, had to perjure himself and violate the law or do without. Mr. Patterson's speech was replete with disclosures which evidently seemed to him very startling. A gentleman who made the count, said he used the expression, "What do you think of that?" 73 times.

Governor McSweeney followed Mr. Patterson. He expressed his pleasure at meeting the people of York county, and said he would much prefer to discuss questions other than liquor; but as Mr. Patterson had devoted so much of his time to the dispensary law and had sought to impress the people with the idea that there was no one else in the state competent to enforce it, he would have to address himself to that subject. "I have been doing all in my power to enforce the dispensary law. My first official act was to address
subject. I have been doing all in my power to enforce the dispensary law. My first official act was to address letters to the sheriffs, mayors and magistrates of the state calling their especial attention to this law and asking them to put forth their best efforts to secure its proper enforcement. I reduced the constabulary one-half, thus saving the state $20,000 a year without any material reduction of the efficiency of the force. I assert that the law has been enforced, during my administration, better than at any time previously since it has been on the statute books, and with less friction. I have no apologies to make for anything I have done in connection with this law. It has my most hearty approval as the best possible solution of the liquor question, and I propose to continue to use my best endeavors to have it enforced. Everybody who knows Charleston, knows that there is no sympathy there for the dispensary law; but when a Charleston grand jury refuses to return true bills on indictments for violation of the dispensary law, how am I to proceed further? And after all, the Charleston grand jury is only on a par with the Barnwell grand jury that refused to return a true bill, on Mr. Patterson's affidavit, against a blind tiger. But I am doing all in Charleston that I could be expected to do. I am willing to apply every known instrument of the law to punish the guilty; but I am not going beyond or outside the law. I am not going to allow constables to enter houses on vague suspicion or do any other unlawful act. I thank God for it that during my administration there has been no bloodshed in connection with the dispensary law, and that there has been no lynching. The dispensary law is more popular today than it has ever been. The people are realizing that there is a great deal in the dispensary law, and I do not believe they will give it up. Even if you had Prohibition under Colonel Hoyt—and you will never have it—what is to prevent the people from sending to Augusta, Charlotte, and other places to get their supplies of liquor for 'personal use?' I say that prohibition has been a failure wherever it has been tried, and you cannot show me a single instance in which it has been a success. I believe it would be better for you if you had several well-regulated dispensaries in this county. [Laughter.] The failure in Kansas will be the failure in this state, and if you try prohibition and find it a failure, as you will, it will take 10 years for you to get back where you are now." NEWS SUMMARY
MONDAY, JULY 23.

State.—The two Florence negroes charged with rape were brought to Columbia for safe keeping.—State campaigners met at Camden.—Will Parker, colored, of Laurens County, killed his wife.—A negro man was killed by lightning near Florence.

Nation.—A negro was lynched at Huntsville, a. Sheriff was nearly suffcated while defending the jail.—Eleven negroes were accidentally drowned at Akron, Ala.

World.—President is willing to mediate between the Chinese government and the powers under certain conditions. Foreign ministers reported alive on the 18th. Conflicting stories continue.

TUESDAY, JULY 24.

State.—State candidates spoke at Kershaw.—State constables captured two distilling. outfits near Young's Store, Laurens County.—Florence citizens held a mass meeting and requested the governor to return the prisoners to Florence. Governor declined to do so.

Nation.—Engineers on the Southern will get an advance of 5 to 10 per cent. in wages.—Desperate negro killed two police officers in New Orleans and wounded a third.—First bale of new crop cotton sold today and brought 161-2 cents.—$750,000 fire in Buffalo, N. Y.

World.—Little additional news from China.

WEDNESDAY, JULY 25.

HOW WILL THEY VOTE?
It is very gratifying to the friends of Prohibition to see their candidate for Governor, Col. James A. Hoyt, so kindly and cordially received wherever he goes, and to note the expressions of the papers predicting his election, but we wish to call the attention of the Prohibitionists to the importance of seeing to it that good men are elected to the Legislature. It is important for the Governor to have the support of the Legislature and the people should see to this now while the candidates are out shaking hands, making speeches and asking for votes. It is not only fair but right to ask a candidate how he proposes to vote on the liquor business if he is elected. Let every candidate define his position; there is no impropriety in this, and it is good morals and good politics. If any man is afraid or ashamed to define his position on this matter he is not the man to represent the people. If he is in favor of the Dispensary, let him say so; if he is in favor of Prohibition, let him say so, for that is the issue now before the people of South Carolina, and the voters will do well to put the question, "Are you going to support the Dispensary, or will you support Prohibition?" That is the question; let the candidates answer it.

DR. MONTAGUE, in a card in another column, calls attention to two important matters, and we hope his suggestions will receive a hearty response from the friends of Furman all over the State. The library of Furman can be greatly helped in the way he suggests. There are many books useful and helpful that might be placed in the library enriching its shelves without impoverishing any one. A thousand or two valuable books might be added to the library every year at small cost to the University or its friends. The other suggestion, that pastors and friends furnish him with the names of young men who may attend college, is of prime importance, and one that should receive a general and hearty response. Now is the time for the president and professors to communicate with young men who may be persuaded to attend Furman. The friends should not wait for some representative of the University to call in person and see these young men. That is not possible in every case, but it is possible to write them a letter, if they are furnished with the names and address. Let the pastors and friends make it their business to look about them in their churches and neighborhoods for the boys and young men who ought to attend Furman, and speak a word to them and then write to Dr. Montague about them. What is done in this work must be done quickly.

WE WISH to commend the course of Governor McSweeney, the sheriff of Florence county and other officials and citizens who aided in the protection of the Negroes arrested and held for trial for a heinous crime. The officers who held the prisoners did right to protect them against all odds. The Governor did right in not acceding to a demand of certain citizens of Florence that the prisoners be sent back to Florence after they had been lodged in the penitentiary for safe-keeping. There was every reason to believe a lynching awaited the prisoners upon their return to Florence, and the officers did exactly right to take no risks. It is not supposed for a moment that the people generally of Florence wished a lynching, but quite the contrary, the law-abiding citizens did not wish it. Possibly there was no danger of a lynching. In any event, when it seemed to the officers that there was danger of mob violence they could not do otherwise than protect their prisoners, and we heartily commend them for their course, and it would be well if such a course could be pursued more frequently, then cur State would not be disgraced by lynchings and mob violence.

HIS ANSWER.
Governor McSweeney Replies to
iCharges Against Him.

HIS REPLY GIVEN IN FULL.

He Defends His Administration
and Presents His Claims for
Re-Election to the Office
of Governor.

Governor McSweeney has prepared a
statement regarding his administration
and position, which is interesting. He
says:

Fellow-Citizens:—In presenting my
claims as a candidate for governor I
desire to thank you for your suffrage
in twice electing me to the responsible
position of lieutenant-governor. In that
position I discharged my duties fairly,
fearlessly and faithfully, and received
the proud endorsement of the body
over which I presided. My platform
has already been announced in my
annual message and on the hustings, but
I shall endeavor to give it to you again,
for I believe the people should hear
fully the candidates asking for their
suffrage. As you know, I succeeded the
lamented Governor Ellerbe to fill out his unexpired term, and I come before you to ask your endorsement. I am one of the people and have fought my way through the world single handed and alone, and I am not ashamed of my record. Ever since I have been in public life I have continuously fought for the people and their rights.

I am an advocate of an ecomical government wisely and judiciously administered with as small a tax as the safe operation of the government will allow. My service has not been lip service, big professions and little deeds, for I have never yet let an opportunity pass to help the young men and young women upward and onward in life, and I have always endeavored to protect and preserve the proud name of my native state, for the proudest heritage that I have is that I am a Carolinian. Nor have my services to the old soldier been wasted in sympathetic speeches, in public and private life I have silently and quietly done all in my power to smooth the road of the tottering Confederate soldier on his final march to the grave.

I am a firm believer in common schools. It is to them that I owe my advancement in life. My education was limited to them; my heart is wrapped up in them, and I would be as traitorous to desert the common schools as the college man would be to accept his alma mater. Starting out in life as an orphan and penniless, the only friend I had was the free public schools. I have taken a special interest in them and shall continue to do so as long as I can be of service to them. I believe that special attention should be given to the education of children at our cotten factories. When I appointed the state board of education some time ago I appointed as a member an able teacher of a school of a manufacturing town in order that the interest of the factory children might have the benefit of his experience, and that they should have a representative on the highest educational board in the state.

Likewise I am a consistent friend of the colleges, both state and denominational. I glory in the proud record our colleges have made in the past and the splendid unlimited future before them. School houses have done more for civilization and Christianity than all the armies of conquest have ever done or can ever do.

The material prosperity of our state is exceedingly gratifying. While this is not due to my administration, for no governor can stop our march of prosperity, yet I have done all in my power to help the grand movement along and to establish confidence in our enterprise and in our state government.

My opponents have attacked me because I subscribed for the newspapers. By such charges they expect to catch the unthinking. Such a charge is an insult to intelligence. All of my predecessors properly subscribed for papers and paid for them in the same way. It is absolutely necessary for the governor to know whether proclamations, advertisements for supplies and so fourth have been published as rail for, and to keep posted as to grand jury presentments, violations of the law, conduct of public officials, riots, lynchings and so forth. Only a few weeks ago a crime was committed in Florence county. The prisoners were arrested, and had it not been that the governor was posted as to the state of feeling at Florence, in a great measure through the newspapers, a crime would have been committed that would have been a foul blot on the good name of our state and an insult to Christianity and a perversion of law and order. And, my friends, I say here in this connection that so long as I am governor that I will exhaust every available means of the state before I will allow a mob law or lynch law to dominate the government and rule the lands.

But we are here to discuss measures and not men. What is local option and what would be the result of such a scheme? It is so impracticable that neither Governor Tillman, nor Evans, nor Ellerbe, all stalwart friends of the dispensary, ever once thought of suggesting such an idea and no honest prohibitionist can favor it for it allows that which he believes to be inherently wrong. The result of such a scheme would be a conglomeration of prohibition and dispensary counties, each bearing the burden and receiving the ill-effect of the other, with no benefits to either. It is a patchwork, crazy quilt, theory and could only result in confusion, and simply lives as a theory,

nor. The greatest evil to the public is the liquor seller. The more he sells the greater his profit. The profit feature is his only incentive and therefore, more the encouragement he offers the buyer to buy more and more. That being the case the best solution is to remove the cause that compels the unfortunate to buy more and more. The dispensary solves this.

The dispenser gets his salary whether he sells one drop or not, and he is not allowed to indulge in the seductive and disastrous credit system. It is of no interest to him to sell impure liquor or to seduce a minor or to give a free lunch to the unwary. He is sworn and bonded to enforce the law and his position is at stake. If he fails to enforce the law, you, the people, who give him his position, can blame only yourselves.

How different is the blind tiger, the progeny of prohibition, whose only ambition is to make dollars for himself and drunkards for the state and whose only claim to citizenship is based on his brazen effrontery as a law breaker. But it is contended there are tigers under the dispensary system. Certainly, but the dispensary law does not make tigers. Do you suppose people patronize tigers because there is a dispensary law, or because they want liquor to drink?

It is the patronage that makes tigers, and is it not natural to conclude that if you abolish the dispensary that the patronage heretofore going to the dispensary will go to the blind tigers, thereby increasing them ten fold.

Then, when the dispensary goes the special officer must go, and with only the civil officers, who are now unable to cope with the few tigers the chaotic condition that must follow is enough to stagger every citizen who loves his home and respects the law.

Under a prohibition law a heavy tax must be levied upon every one to enforce the law whether he favors prohibition or not. But under the law every trifling negro who buys his flask of liquor contributes a tax to the town and county to see that he keeps the peace, to work the road and to educate the children.

Prohibition is a beautiful sentiment, but a miserable failure in practice. The prohibitionist can use no stronger argument than to cite the states that have tried prohibition. Maine—Number of retail liquor dealers 1,125

Iowa—Number of retail liquor dealers 3,730.

South Carolina—Number of retail liquor dealers 324

Shot by a Neyro
Cheneyville, La., August 10.—In a shooting here this afternoon Benny Wall, aged 21, was shot and killed by Joseph Hamilton, a negro. The latter was severely wounded, having his leg broken by one of Wall's bullets. Hamilton was arrested. Nothing is known about the cause of the trouble between the two men.
joe-milton-cheneyville-1900-08-13.A2:
RACE DIFFICULTY LEADS TO BLOODSHED.
YOUNG WHITE MAN KILLED BY LOUISIANA NEGRO-LYNCHING PREVENTED.
YOUNG WHITE MAN KILLED BY LOUISIANA
NEGRO—LYNCHING PREVENTED.

New-Orleans, Aug. 11 (Special).—The incompatibility of the white and black races led to the killing of a young white man to-day and the serious wounding of a negro. The affair occurred at Cheneyville, La. Benjamin Wall and Samuel Blum, young white men, were walking on a plankwalk from Cheneyville to Theoda. The walk consists of two narrow boards side by side. Half way between the two settlements Wall and Blum met a negro named Joseph Milton, who was out walking with his sweetheart. Blum and Wall stepped to the left, walking single file, but the negroes refused to unlock arms, and Milton brushed heavily against Wall. The white man resented the conduct with a blow. Milton walked a few steps and drew a revolver. Wall followed suit, and a pistol duel followed, each firing four shots. Wall's abdomen was penetrated, and he died in a few minutes. Milton's leg was broken and he crawled away into a cornfield. A crowd of enraged whites quickly collected, and it was with great difficulty that a lynching was averted and the negro carried to jail at Alexandria. Wall was a prominent young man.
joe-milton-cheneyville-1900-08-13.A3:
TO REGULATE NEGROES' CONDUCT. Whites of a Louisiana Parish Meet and Lay Down Rules for Various Situations.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Aug. 13.—Because of the killing of a white man, Bennie Wall, by a negro, Joe Milton, the white people of Cheney Rapids Parish have met in a public meeting and decided upon a number of rules relative to the future conduct and discipline of the negroes in that region. There was a disposition shown at first to attempt to lynch Milton, and squads of armed white men from Bunkle, Alexandria, Haasville, Iamourie and other places rode into Cheneyville and tendered their assistance. The Sheriff of the parish, however, stood firm in his determination to allow no lynching; and the regulators who rode into town were told that their services were not needed.

It was then decided to hold a conference of white residents of Cheneyville to decide upon measures to preserve peace and order. C. Cannon was called to the chair, R. H. Jackson chosen secretary. A committee of five was appointed to prepare resolutions. All negro men, idle or out of work, were ordered to leave Cheneyville. All barrooms or places where the negroes gamble by day or night, were ordered closed. All negroes found discharging firearms were to be dealt with properly and their weapons taken from them. Other resolutions are as follows:

"Whereas it is a habit of numerous negroes to congregate and sit on the depot, preventing the passage of ladies and children in entering and leaving the depot and cars, be it "Resolved that said custom be immediately abolished; that as there exists an indisposition among a saucy and impudent set of young negro men and women to yield the sidewalks and road to ladies and children, any one caught falling to do so, on being reported to the committee, shall be severely dealt with."

A committee of twenty-two was appointed to see that these resolutions be carried out, and it proceeded at once to close a number of establishments at which the negroes congregate, and to warn idle negroes to leave town. Quite an emigration set in at once. Cheneyville is the place that figures conspicuously in "Uncle Tom's Cabin."

MR. EDITOR:
The quiet little item headed "A Shooting Affray in Cheneyville" which appeared in the Texas and Shreveport papers gave little idea of the exciting events that transpired there on Friday evening last. A shove by the negro, a blow from the white man, a drawing of pistols and exchange of shots, the instant death of the white man, and the cry, "Benny Wall has been killed by a nigger, he's hiding in the cane field," aroused the fury of the neighborhood and gathered an armed mob bent on finishing up the negro. Their trailing him with lanterns through the cane field that night by the track left by his broken leg, his emptying his revolver at his pursuers, the fusillade which announced his capture (listeners were certain it meant his death) all furnished an experience not wholly unfamiliar to your readers. Considering the temper of the mob the negro's escape from lynching is surprising. And a heated controversy between the few who opposed it and the angry numbers who favored dispatching him as the darkey lay upon the platform listening, formed an exciting, though not an enjoyable entertain-
Fortunately the T. and P. agent there, Mr. Frank Hanley, who by the way, is a son of our kind friend Mrs. P. Hanley, had thoughtfully attended to all preliminaries of tickets and baggage early in the evening and no confusion or delay was occasioned to passengers by the subsequent occurrences. Indeed this was but one instance of the courteous attention which the officials of that road uniformily extend towards those who travel over it.

Leaving Cheneyville, we went through Alexandria, the best advertised town in the State, and passed Shreveport, the most progressive and enterprising of our cities. The T. & P. road follows the course of the most stirring campaign which occurred in Louisiana during the Civil War, the retreat of General Taylor before Banks's army, and borders upon the battle fields of Mansfield and Pleasant Hill. These were the two great conflicts between the opposing armies, and the former was one of the most brilliant successes of the confederacy. Had it resulted in a victory for Banks, the battle-field would long ago have been made a national park. But to day there is to the ordinary eye nothing to distinguish these spots as places where history was made.

Between Mansfield and Shreveport lies the Klingman nursery which is probably the largest in Louisiana. The extent of the peach department is particularly noticeable. A Shreveport attorney of high character and standing directed attention to its extent, adding that according to report Mr. Klingman sometimes orders a car-load of peach stones at a time for planting. The statement sounds extravagent but the young trees are growing about as close together as corn is usually dropped with us and it doubtless takes many stones to plant an extensive field of trees. One Texas point of interest to some of our good people is Scottville where are located the grounds of the Holiness Camp Meeting. The meeting itself had closed the previous Sunday. At Marshall, a town of 10,000, a $65, 000 court house is in course of erection, and the people are in good spirits over the large car shops now being built there by the T. & P. At Fort Worth we found the handsomest depot one could

Long Way to Save a Negro
Jackson, Miss., Aug. 8.—Sheriff Harding and a posse of deputies started today to Pocahontas, sixteen miles distant, in response to a message, that a mob was gathering to lynch a negro named Jones, who was arrested yesterday, charged with assaulting a white woman. Trouble is feared.

RACE RIOT AT GREENVILLE.
Negro Precipitates a Difficulty—Severl Shots Fired—One Man Wounded.
Negro Precipitates a Difficulty—Severl Shots Fired—One Man Wounded.

GREENVILLE, S. C., Aug. 15.—At the Monaghan cotton mill, which is being built just outside of town, a nogro laborer, Bill Thompson, and another negro had a fight. The superintendent of construction, a white man from the north, parted the negroes. Thompson cursed him. The superintendent ordered Thompson off the place, but a short time afterward the negro again cursed him and threw a rock at the superintendent, who received the missile on his arm. The white bosses then chased Thompson, and several shots were fired by both whites and negroes, the negroes being better armed than the whites.

Thompson was shot in the neck, but not seriously hurt. After this nearly all the negro laborers quit work.
tom-koeh-greenville-1900-08-15.A4:
A RACE RIOT
AVERTED AT MONAGHAN MILLS TUESDAY BY SENSIBLE WHITE MEN.
Brutal Attack on Superintendent McNalley by Furious Negroes-One Negro Shot Nearly Two Hundred Negroes Ready for Blood.
[Greenville News, 15th.]

by the action of a few conservative white men, a serious race riot was narrowly averted yesterday morning at the Monaghan mills located about two miles from the city.

The Flint Building and Construction Company has the contract for building the mills and employs about fifty white and nearly 20000 workmen culminated in a trifling dispute between two of the new workmen culminated in a fist fight. A. F. McNally, superintendent of the Flint Construction Company, attempted to separate the negroes and secure peace when one of them, Bill Thompson, made an attack upon him. In order to avoid any trouble, Mr. McNalley ordered Thompson to leave the premises.

Thompson then began cursing Mr. McNally, at the same time catching up a rock weighing four or five pounds, and with considerable force hurled it at Mr. McNally, striking him on the arm and causing a serious injury. The rock, in all probability, would have struck Mr. McNally on the head and killed him had he not threw up his arm in time to protect himself.

After throwing the rock Thompson ran and a half dozen white men, who saw him attempt to kill Mr. McNally, started after him. In the pursuit several shots were fired at Thompson, one bullet hitting him in the right jaw and lodging in the left side of the neck.

When it was learned that Thompson had been shot all the negroes quit work, gathered hatchets, axes, rocks and many of them having pistols. The negroes seethed and surged and went round muttering and demanded the victim of their vengeance in a loud and boisterous manner. For a time it appeared that there would be a bloody battle between whites and negroes. The white men, while they kept a close eye on the negroes, exercised splendid judgment and by skillful maneuvering prevented any overt act by the negroes, and things quieted down.

All the negroes, however, quit work, but it is thought by those in a position to know, that they will resume their labors in a few days at most. Among the crowd of negroes there is a number of them hard working and sober-minded and, it is thought, that when they realize that they are upholding by their action one without doubt in the wrong they will come back to their work.

For a brief time it seemed that a bloody riot would result, as the negroes were extremely bitter and abusive and were apparently determined to force a fight.

Greenville, S. C.
What came near being a riot, over two hundred colored men went on a strike at the Monogham mills. Two of them got in a dispute, had a few words and settled it. Foreman McNally cursed one of them and was told that it was no white man's business. At this the white man struck the colored man. After he had received a good thrashing at the hands of the colored man, a number of white men came with sticks and guns to his aid. The colored man ran just as his friends were coming to his rescue. He was shot at four times, one bullet taking effect in his right jaw. All men of color threw down his work and called for time.
